culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Bhutan has conservative standards of dress and behaviour. Take care not to offend. If you visit temples or other religious institutions, dress modestly and respectfully. Long pants are most appropriate for men. Long skirts are most appropriate for women. Bhutan's official tourism site: at dzongs, temples and other sacred sites, wear long sleeves and cover your legs, take off hats, and remove shoes where asked. Don't photograph inside sacred spaces or touch religious objects.

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: Under Bhutan's UAS Regulation 2017, only government organisations may own or operate drones. Private people and companies, including tourists, may not; drone import permits go only to government agencies.

items.text: No public operator register was found; the BCAA says it does not issue drone pilot licences or certificates.

A government operator registers the drone (forwarding letter, Appendix I, fee, technical specifications), then applies for an Unmanned Aircraft Operation Permit with clearances by location (Ministry of Home Affairs for heritage sites, Forests and Park Services for protected areas, Royal Bhutan Police for security-sensitive areas, Royal Bhutan Army for no-fly zones) and evidence of skill, which can be a foreign drone licence or training certificate.

The BCAA FAQ says private individuals or companies are not allowed to own or use drones in Bhutan, and that no agency or individual may import a drone without prior BCAA approval; a drone brought in as a tourist would be seized at the point of entry. Import permits are issued only to government agencies.
